draft.title: Embodied carbon in trade
card: Embodied carbon is the emissions released in making and moving a product. This covers mining, factory energy and shipping.
The emissions are counted in the country where the product is made, not where it is used.
So when a country imports goods, the emissions from making them appear in the exporting country's totals.
This can make a country that imports many goods look cleaner than its buying habits really are.
draft.remember: Embodied carbon is counted where a product is made, not where it is used.

a.q: A shop in Geelong sells a jacket made in Vietnam. Where are the emissions from making it counted?
opts: In Vietnam, where it was made
In Australia, where it is sold
Half in each country
In neither country
a.why: Emissions from making a product are counted in the country that made it. Australia is wrong because the jacket's buyer is not where the emissions were released.

b.q: Country X closes its factories and imports most of its goods from Asia. What is likely to happen to the emissions that X reports?
opts: They fall, though its buying may not have changed
They rise, because it now buys more goods
They stay the same, because the goods are the same
They fall, because it now buys fewer goods
b.why: Emissions from making the goods are now counted in the exporting countries, so X's reported total falls. The last option is wrong because the scenario says nothing about buying less.
b.clue: Ask where the factory emissions are counted now.

a.best: In Vietnam, where it was made

b.best: They fall, though its buying may not have changed

problems.detail: The card says embodied carbon covers shipping, then says 'the emissions' are counted in the country where the product is made. Under national (UNFCCC) reporting, emissions from international shipping fuel are reported separately and are not counted in the exporting country's totals. Either limit the counting line to the emissions from making the product, or note that international shipping is reported separately.

proposal.title: Embodied carbon in trade
card: Embodied carbon is the emissions released in making and moving a product. This covers mining, factory energy and shipping.
Emissions from making a product are counted in the country where it is made, not where it is used. Emissions from international shipping are reported separately, outside any one country's total.
So when a country imports goods, the emissions from making them appear in the exporting country's totals.
This can make a country that imports many goods look cleaner than its buying habits really are.
proposal.remember: Making emissions count where a product is made, not where it is used.

a.q: A shop in Geelong sells a jacket made in Vietnam. Where are the emissions from making it counted?
opts: In Vietnam, where it was made
In Australia, where it is sold
Split evenly between the two countries
In neither country, as it was traded
a.why: Emissions from making a product are counted in the country that made it, so they go in Vietnam's total. Australia is wrong because selling or using the jacket there does not move the making emissions into Australia's total.

b.q: Country X closes its factories and imports most of its goods from Asia. What is likely to happen to the emissions that X reports?
opts: They fall, though its buying may not have changed
They rise, because it now buys more goods
They stay the same, because the goods are the same
They fall, because it now buys fewer goods
b.why: Emissions from making the goods are now counted in the exporting countries, so X's reported total falls. The last option is wrong because the scenario says nothing about buying less: the fall comes from where the goods are made.
b.clue: Ask where the factory emissions are counted now.
